title: Determination of Structure-Property Relationships for Polysaccharide Hydrogels via Correlated Electron Microscopy and Ultra-Small-Angle Neutron Scattering
content: Polysaccharides are among the most-commonly used family of polymer in the world due to the lower critical solution temperature (LCST) behavior of many cellulose-derivatives. The LCST behavior allows for the viscosity to increase as a function of temperature and has made these class of polymers excellent candidates for additives in cosmetics, food packaging, and the pharmaceutical industry. Despite their extensive use, the origins of their mechanical properties has been widely debated. Specifically, the most heavily studied of these classes of materials are methylcellulose (MC) and hydroxypropylmethylcellulose (HPMC) [1-4]. MC is a water-soluble semi-flexible polymer at low temperatures and transitions into a turbid gel at temperatures greater than the lower critical solution temperature (LCST) (Figure 1A and 1B) [5-8]. Over the last decade, cryogenic TEM (cryo-TEM) and bulk small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) techniques have shown that gelation results from the self-assembly of MC chains into ∼20 nm diameter fibrils, which then arrange into a physical gel (Figure 1C) [2, 4, 9, 10]. Following this discovery, cryo-TEM supported the argument that the rheological properties of these randomly percolated fibrillar networks could be related to the previously established model of semiflexible biopolymer networks [11]. Yet, due to the resolution limitations of conventional cryo-TEM and the disturbance of the fibril network inherent to sample preparation, the mechanism of assembly of the MC chains within the fibrils and the assembly of the fibrils into network have yet to be revealed by real-space techniques [12]. Furthermore, these same artifacts have prevented the direct observation of the native gel structure. To study the sol-gel phase transition of MC and other LCST polysaccharides, we have utilized variable temperature liquid cell transmission electron microscopy (VT-LCTEM), an in situ imaging technique that enables high resolution insight into solvated nanomaterials.
